messages.subject: Script for automated graph creation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been asked to summarize the outcomes of the last edition of our
periodic rating of faculty. It was a very short survey (7 questions, 5-
step scale each). So now I have them packed up into data frame, that's
how it looks:

'data.frame':	1623 obs. of  9 variables:
 $ KOD.PRZEDM : Factor w/ 60 levels "128890","128935",..: 36 36 36 36
36 36 36 36 36 36 ...
 $ PYTANIE.1  : int  4 3 4 4 4 4 4 3 4 4 ...
 $ PYTANIE.2  : int  4 3 4 4 4 3 4 2 4 3 ...
 $ PYTANIE.3  : int  4 NA 4 4 4 2 4 5 3 4 ...
 $ PYTANIE.4  : int  5 4 4 5 4 4 4 1 4 5 ...
 $ PYTANIE.5  : int  3 1 3 1 4 3 4 1 3 4 ...
 $ PYTANIE.6  : num  3 3 4 6 3 4 5 4 4 5 ...
 $ PYTANIE.7  : num  90 50 90 90 50 50 30 90 50 90 ...
 $ PYTANIE.7.f: Ord.factor w/ 5 levels "do 20%"<"do 40%"<..: 5 3 5 5 3
3 2 5 3 5 ...

So there are data from each question ("pytanie" means question in
Polish), question #7 is coded as a ordered factor and numeric variable
(median of each interval actually). First variable KOD.PRZEDM is a
factor which is a coded seminar name.
Most important thing is to show each member of faculty his or her
score in questions 1 to 5. I can do it manually, but there are 60
seminars, and 5 scores for each, so it is a lot of work - maybe I can
automate the process? I've tried to utilize a loop here:

for (i in ank$KOD.PRZEDM)
{
qplot(ank$PYTANIE.1, data=subset(ank.na <http://ank.na>==i), geom="histogram", breaks=c
(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), main="Distribution for question 1, for i seminar")
qsave(filename="i.png", dpi=72)
}

But it fails do work properly - I'm unable to pass the loop variable
"i" to the filename and the main title of the graph - I would be
grateful for help.

I also wondered whether or not a loop in loop is possible to create
all graphs at once? Like...

for (i in ank$KOD.PRZEDM)
	{
		for (k in 1:5)
		{
		qplot(ank$PYTANIE.k, data=subset(ank.na <http://ank.na>==i),
 		geom="histogram", 	breaks=c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
		main="Distribution for question k, 	for i seminar")
		qsave(filename="seminar_i_question_k.png", dpi=72)
		}
	}

I also thought about personalized information "me vs the rest of the
staff" which would be a box and whisker (me) inside / next to bigger
box and whisker (rest of the faculty) (???), but that is way, wayyy
beyond my current abilities - I'm a rookie :-)

Kamil

messages.subject: transforming scales discretely
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

It is often interesting when displaying time series to put emphasis on
the display of more recent figures.  This is often done by using, for
example 3/4 of the horizontal space with one scale (displaying for
example the time series over the last few years, excluding observation
from the last month) and 1/4 with a "higher" frequency (displaying the
series over the last month).  This permits to contemplate both the
more recent movements in more detail as well as to keep this movements
"in perspective".  If this possible in ggplot2, possibly transforming
the time scale somehow?  Many thanks in advance for your help.
Kind regards,
Ivan

messages.subject: Ordering of factors in (aesthetics/legends)
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,
I have come across a bug in ggplot2. Any help you can provide will be
helpful.

The bug involves inconsistent assigning of aesthestics to factor/
character data. I am trying to produce many individual plots from
multiple data sets. As in the example below, my factor/character data
is constant over the data sets (see ctry), but may be randomly
ordered. When producing multiple plots, the aesthetics seem to "train"
themselves in the order that the data is encountered. This is
different than how as.factor would treat the data. as.factor first
sorts the data and then assigns levels.

<CODE>

require(ggplot2)

# Code to illustrate mis-ordering of factors on different plots.
# Seems to set "aes" based on order, not level of as.factor(data)

ctry <- rep(c("US","UK", "EU", "JP"), each = 5)
x <- (runif(20) - 1 * 5)
y <- (runif(20) - 1 * 5)

plotData <- data.frame(ctry, x, y, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sapply(plotData, class)

p1 <- qplot(x, y, data = plotData, geom="point", colour = ctry)
p2 <- qplot(x, y, data = plotData[order(plotData$ctry), ],
geom="point", colour = ctry)

plotData.f <- plotData
plotData.f[, "ctry"] <- as.factor(plotData.f[, "ctry"])
sapply(plotData.f, class)

p1.f <- qplot(x, y, data = plotData.f, geom="point", colour = ctry)
p2.f <- qplot(x, y, data = plotData.f[order(plotData.f$ctry), ],
geom="point", colour = ctry)

# How as.factor treats the data
# note that kk assigns level 1 to "BR", as does ll ---> consistent
treatment
# regardless of data order
kk <- as.factor(plotData[, "ctry"])
ll <- as.factor(plotData[order(plotData$ctry), "ctry"])

# i386-apple-darwin8.11.1

messages.subject: Problems with ggsave(type = "pdf") on Mac
messages.body_plain:

Mac (see sessionInfo below), linetype = 5, or at least the fifth

properly onscreen in an R session, but does not display properly in
the pdf.

messages.subject: Bug: geom reevaluates args
messages.body_plain:
qplot(rexp(10),rexp(10)) + geom_rug()

has the rugmarks in random (literally!) places, but rug seems to work fine for deterministic y's like sin(1:10).

I will guess that this is because it is re-evaluating rexp(10) rather than calculating the values once and reusing them.

Besides the problem in this non-deterministic case, I suppose this would also be a problem if the calculation were expensive.

I do realize that it is much better form, though, to precalculate the values and save them in a data frame.

         -s

R 2.8.0
Windows Vista

messages.subject: Smoothed quantile plot
messages.body_plain:
I'm looking for a way of calculating and plotting smoothed quantiles.

Suppose I teach archery, and I want to plot the progress of students as they get more and more practice.  I want to plot not only the fitted improvement line, but also see what the distribution of marksmanship is like at any given experience level.  So I collect snapshot data for all my students: as of today, how many times have you shot at the target? And how many times have you hit it? (Yes, there are issues around drop-outs and so on, but let's leave that aside for now.) So I make a scatterplot of (hit count)/(try count) against (try count).  Oh, and by the way, the distribution of (try count) is highly skewed -- most of the students have only tried 1-3 times, though a few students have tried as many as 1000 times.

A first look at the data shows that a linear quantile regression doesn't capture the data very well, so I want to plot some sort of smoothed quantile. I could certainly bin the data and calculate the quantiles for each bin, but I'd rather have a smooth estimate.

What would be a sensible way of smoothing this data so that I can visualize it?  If expect a priori that the quality of marksmanship will improve monotonically with experience, can I use that fact to smooth better?

What I have in mind is some sort of running quantile calculation weighted by a kernel function.  If there's nothing standard along those lines, I'll try my hand at it, but I'm sure my solution would take much longer to write, run inefficiently, and probably not be statistically/mathematically as sound as something that exists already!

Thanks!

           -s

messages.body_plain:
I see what you are saying (hey, the reply-to worked too :)

I'd sometimes like to be able to do this too, I graph events and
sometimes they come fast and furious, and I've thought about
stretching time in those sections.

I can't quite get my head around what would make a sensible
interface.  Eventually time series are turned into X-Y plots and the
breaks/labels are applied (think of the X axis actually being a large
count, like seconds since 1970 or something similar).  So you'd want
to specify parts of the time-series where the spaces on the X axis
represented different periods of time (i.e. numbers of seconds), and
then get the labels right as well.  To do this in any arbitrary manner
seems pretty tough to me.

Perhaps one could provide an array of breaks, each being a date, and
then communicate that you wanted those to be equally spaced on the X
axis (e.g. "2007-01-01, 2007-02-01, 2007-03-01, 2007-04-01,
2007-04-02, 2007-04-03, ...).  The method, something like a
specialized subset, would then need to make a new XY graph, with the
appropriate values for those dates taken from the data-frame, and that
set of labels.  Seems like that could be written externally to
ggplot2, just passing in the new series not as a Date series, though.

> I can't quite get my head around what would make a sensible
> interface.  Eventually time series are turned into X-Y plots and the
> breaks/labels are applied (think of the X axis actually being a large
> count, like seconds since 1970 or something similar).  So you'd want
> to specify parts of the time-series where the spaces on the X axis
> represented different periods of time (i.e. numbers of seconds), and
> then get the labels right as well.  To do this in any arbitrary manner
> seems pretty tough to me.
>
> Perhaps one could provide an array of breaks, each being a date, and
> then communicate that you wanted those to be equally spaced on the X
> axis (e.g. "2007-01-01, 2007-02-01, 2007-03-01, 2007-04-01,
> 2007-04-02, 2007-04-03, ...).  The method, something like a
> specialized subset, would then need to make a new XY graph, with the
> appropriate values for those dates taken from the data-frame, and that
> set of labels.  Seems like that could be written externally to
> ggplot2, just passing in the new series not as a Date series, though.

A similar transformation is when you are plotting financial (or other
data) when you want to remove weekends and public holidays.  I've done
this a few times by converting the dates to numeric, munging them in
some way, and then adding a custom continuous scale with appropriate
breaks and labels.  I've never figured out a good generalisation
(instead doing the transformation "by hand" each time), but this would
be very useful.

Hadley

I hope it's OK to ask about ggplot here; I see ggplot2 is still in beta
so I thought my life would be easier with ggplot.

I have several different categories of data, identified by the variable
"type."  I want a plot in which plots of the different types are
superimposed.  Each individual plot should have lines connecting its
points.  The problem is that the lines insist on connecting points
belonging to different types.

I tried
qplot(x=beta1, y=reject, data=b1, facets = varb~nsamp, type=c("line",
"point"), colour=type, linetype=type)

b1 has sections stacked vertically with the different types, i.e., first
all entries for one type appear, then the next, and so on.

"line" is supposed to go left to right; it does, but it passes through
points of each type along the way.

I also tried "paths" for plot type; this is a bit better, but it draws a
line back from the one of one type (that's my type variable, not the
plot type) to the start of the next.

Is there a way to get what I want, which is the logic of "line" applied
separately to each type?

Thanks.
Ross

ggplot 0.4.1; R 2.7.1 on Debian GNU/Linux.  I originally installed
ggplot and related packages June 2007; I've reinstalled ggplot, but not
the others, under my current R.

The root of your problems is probably an old version of R.  Upgrade,

Hadley

messages.subject: Error bar question
messages.body_plain:
Hello folks,

I'm a long time programmer, and an academic, that dabbles in
statistical analysis for many of my experiments. I've been wanting to
replace SPSS and sigma plot with R for some time, and just finished
reading R for SAS and SPSS users, which was fantastic. But, I just
finished some very easy statistical analysis, and I'm trying to
generate some error bar graphs that match my existing publications to
make sure I'm doing everything right. These graphics are "basically"
working, but I'm not quite grasping how to get them to look how I
want.

Specifically, I have an error bar graph that is generated using the
following code:

#Error bars for Atotal
ggplot(math,
  aes( as.numeric(Group), Atotal) ) +
  stat_summary(fun.y="mean",
    geom="smooth", se=FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal",
    geom="errorbar", width=.2) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits=c("No Pauses", "Pauses"), name="Participant
Group") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,200), name = "Total Rating")
ggsave(file = "math/Atotal.eps")

This generally works, but has a few things I would like to change.

1. As far as I can tell, the error bars are representing standard
deviation, but I would prefer (for this particular publication) if
they presented standard error of the mean instead. My assumption was
that by changing se=FALSE to se=TRUE, that this would change the
stat_summary function to mean standard error, but when I generate the
graph, it doesn't appear to visually change, and I don't see "se"
mentioned in the documentation anywhere at:

http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_summary.html

2. I would "prefer" to remove the grey background and replace it with
a white one with a black border around the entire graphic.

3. as.numeric(Group) refers to two discrete groups. The mean of each
group is connected via a bright blue line. Many publications do not
allow color. Any way to make this line black instead of blue?

4. When I call scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,200), name = "Total
Rating"), my assumption was that it would scale the graph between
those values. It does do this, sort of, but it leaves a small buffer
above 200 and below zero. Any way to remove this?

Maybe these are dumb questions (I'm still an R beginner, after all),
so I apologize in advance, but hopefully someone out there has some
ideas.

Thanks in advance,

Andreas

messages.subject: ggplot2 derivative: aov_plot()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My colleagues lament the passing of StatView, an OS 9 app that
provided rather simple yet powerful abilities to plot data for a given
effect from a factorial ANOVA. To facilitate their conversion to R,
I've attempted to replicate this in a function called aov_plot().

I'd be interested to get input from anyone that might find this
interesting/useful. I've uploaded the current version of the code to:
http://drop.io/aov_plot

- aov_plot.R contains the code and description of aov_plot()

- demo.R contains a demo of using aov_plot on data similar to that
obtained from the Attention Network Test

- generate_demo_data.R contains code for generating data necessary for
running demo.R

Note that the default error bars I've chosen represent Fisher's Least
Significant Difference. In the context of purely within or between
effects, these bars facilitate post-hoc multiple comparison (if the
bars of any two points fail to overlap, the points may be considered
significantly different at alpha=.05). However, I've been told that
they can not be used in this manner in the context of mixed between &
within effects. In absence of consensus on an alternative for these
cases, I chose to plot the FLSD bars but suggest that use of such
plots should also contain a footnote noting that the bars can not be
used for post-hoc multiple comparison. In the future I may change my
mind on this and instead simply plot no error bars in such
circumstances.

Cheers,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar:
http://tinyurl.com/mikes-public-calendar

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

Yes, the problem is that the standard error of the means maybe almost
completely unrelated to the standard errors of the differences between

most interest.

not be a flawless file. In my case,

up the whole space while the

(alpha =0.4) was gone in the PNG

messages.subject: Re: scale_y_continuous and geom_text questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Herbert -

For the y axis label, I am supposing that you are using the black and white theme set, i.e., theme_bw() (it has that problem).  To fix it, as Hadley suggested a few days ago, this should work

theme_set(theme_bw())  ## this sets the theme as theme_bw()
theme_update(axis.title.y =
  theme_text(size = 12, angle = 90, vjust = 0.5)) ## this updates it so that the text is in the right place

For the rest, I am not sure that I understand what you want to do, but perhaps the gist is in some of the following examples :

srda <- dat <- read.table(textConnection('   Thresh Time Color Intens Seen        rFit        gFit

1        1    0   RED    0.8    1  0.11033208  1.94633102
2        1    2   RED    0.2    1  0.01516950  1.69396036
3        1    3   RED   -0.4    1 -0.02895994  1.57692931
4        1    4   RED   -1.0    1 -0.07093717  1.46560594
8        1    8   RED   -1.0    1 -0.21934788  1.07202154
11       1   11   RED   -1.2    1 -0.31271811  0.82440417

15       1   16   RED   -1.2    1 -0.44033896  0.48595437'))

molten_srda <- melt(srda, id = c('Thresh', 'Time', 'Color', 'Intens', 'Seen'))

y_title <- expression('Intensity,  ' * cd/m^2)
p <- ggplot(srda) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Time (ms)", limits = c(0, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = y_title, limits = c(-10,3)) +
  geom_point(aes(Time, Intens), colour = 'red') +
  geom_line(aes(x = Time, y = value, colour = variable), data = molten_srda)
p

tt <- data.frame(
  x <- seq(0, 16, by = 4),
  y <- seq(-8, 2, length = 5),
  text <- c(letters[1:5]),
  text_size <- 5*(1:5)
)

p1 <- p + geom_text(data=tt,aes(x=x,y=y,label=text, size = text_size))
p1

p2 <- p + geom_text(data=tt,aes(x=x,y=y,label=text), size = 10)
p2

To change the labels and title in the legend, you can use something like :

  scale_colour_discrete('Fit', labels = c('Red', 'Green'))

Hope it helps!
david.

messages.subject: Re: cannot get png looking correctly
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I also had big problems to generate correct looking png-files with
complicated figures. I finally gave up and used a not very elegant but
very efficient work around (only applicable for windows users). Just
save your figures as pdf-files. Install the freely available PDF-
XChange Viewer. It's much better than adobe reader anyway.
http://www.docu-track.com/home/prod_user/PDF-XChange_Tools/pdfx_viewer

Open the pdf-file in the XChange Viewer and save it in any format and
resolution you want (including png among others). I has always given
me perfect results so far.

Cheers,
Erich

messages.body_plain:
Hi:
I'm trying to plot data (in the x-y plane)  associated with 9
different classes of data, with each class having its own color.
Normally, I would use scale_colour_brewer( )  + scale_color_hue(alpha
= X ) to change the alpha level of the points.  This approach has
worked great before. However, with my current data set I get an error
message stating:

"Error: scale_brewer can deal with a maximum of 8 discrete values, but
you have 9.  See ?scale_manual for a possible alternative "

==== Aside ====
I can get a plot to appear if scale_colour_brewer( ) has an argument
or arguments, but I cannot change the color palettes as in
scale_colour_brewer(type="seq", palette=3)  with my 9 class data set.
There is no error message generated though. As a matter of fact, it
really doesn't matter what is used as an argument in between the
parentheses  for  scale_colour_brewer(type="seq", palette=3) or
scale_colour_brewer(type="qualitative", palette=1), the plot remains
unchanged.
==============

Given the error message generated, above, I successfully assigned  the
colors of the classes that I desired using :

scale_colour_manual(values = c
("magenta","pink","brown","yellow","orange","purple","green","blue","red"))

My question is: How do I change the alpha levels of these points when
using  scale_colour_manual( ) ?

Thanks,
Greg

messages.subject: correlation matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm attempting to plot a correlation matrix similar to (but not
precisely replicating) the one found here:
http://addictedtor.free.fr/graphiques/RGraphGallery.php?graph=152

I think the continuous color is redundant to the continuous size, so I
think I'll just go with black for negative correlations and white for
positive correlations. Below is my attempt in ggplot, but I'm having
trouble:

1. ensuring size defines the *area* of the circle

2. ensuring the size of a point reflecting a correlation of 1 is such
that is just touches the bounds of its bin (i.e., if it's in row1, it
spans from 0.5 to 1.5 on the x-axis)

library(ggplot2)

mat = matrix(rnorm(100),10,10)

ggplot(
	melt(cor(mat))
	,aes(
		x=X1
		,y=X2
		,size=abs(value)
		,colour=I(ifelse(value>0,'white','black'))
	)
)+
geom_point()+
scale_colour_manual(values=c('white','black'))+
labs(
	y=''
	,x=''
)+
opts(
	panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()
	,panel.grid.major = theme_blank()
	,legend.position = 'none'
	,axis.text.x = theme_text(hjust=1,angle=90)
)

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student

messages.subject: scale_hue vs colorspace
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I would expect the fill colours of the following plots to be
identical, as the arguments are the same, but they are not.
Am I missing something or is it that scale_fill_hue is not directly
compatible with colorspace rainbow_hcl function?

Thanks.

===
library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)

df <- data.frame(x=letters[1:4], y=1)
p <- qplot(data=df, x, y, geom="bar", stat="identity", fill=x)
p1 <- p + scale_fill_hue(h=c(30, 300), c = 50, l = 70) + opts
(title="fill_hue")

colours <- rainbow_hcl(4,  c = 50, l = 70, start = 30, end = 300)
p2 <- p + scale_fill_manual (values=colours) + opts
(title="fill_manual")

vplayout <- function(x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(2,1)))
print(p1, vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(p2, vp=vplayout(2,1))

--

messages.subject: Re: scale_hue vs colorspace
messages.body_plain:
It's because scale_fill_hue generates n + 1 colours between start and
end and then drops the last colour.  That's the best method I could
come up with for when you have n colours spanning 0 to 360, but it's
not quite right when you restrict the range of the hues.

Maybe when start and end are equal (mod 360), I should subtract 360/n
from the end point.

Hadley

messages.subject: Removing slashes in legend?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is there a way to set a border around bars such that the corresponding
swatches in the legend don't get slashes (diagonal lines) through
them?

An example of what I'm talking about is:

    http://freya.cs.uiuc.edu/~njriley/slash.pdf

The plot command I'm using is:

    ggplot(runtimes, aes(x='', fill=variants, y=speedup)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept=1, colour='grey50') +
      geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge', colour='black',
size=0.25) +
      opts(axis.title.x=theme_blank()) +
      facet_grid(. ~ bench) +
      scale_x_discrete(NULL, breaks=NA) +
      scale_y_log2('Speedup vs. CPython 2.4.3',
                   breaks=breaks, labels=format(breaks,
drop0trailing=TRUE)) +
      opts(plot.margin = unit(c(0, 0, -2, 0), "lines")) +
      scale_fill_manual(values=colors)

Thanks.

messages.subject: Fwd: [R] plotting effect confidence intervals
messages.body_plain:
The note to R-help below is from a colleague of mine who raises an
interesting conundrum and I thought individuals on this list might
have some ideas.

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: John Christie <John.C...@dal.ca>
Date: Fri, Apr 17, 2009 at 8:51 PM
Subject: [R] plotting effect confidence intervals
To: R-h...@r-project.org

Hi,

I'm trying to work out plotting effect confidence intervals for a
mixed effects design.  For example, when measuring heights over age
one will get two kinds of confidence intervals from the resulting
model (using intervals in lme), a broad inference interval from the
random intercept, and a narrow inference interval about the fixed
effect slope.

I've been considering what this confidence interval about only the
slope means in a graphical way and am asking for advice.  I know that
in a standard linear model one can make sort of curved dashed lines a
la Prism's plotting capabilities (something I haven't seen in R).  But
I'm not sure this makes sense because it would mean conflating two
kinds of variance I want to keep separate.  In a regular regression
the intercept and slope have similar inference qualities.  But, in
repeated measures mixed effects models the slope (narrow inference
about effect only) will likely be a different kind of inference than
the intercept (absolute value measurement).  Therefore combining those
two to make traditional curves seems inappropriate, especially for
undertanding the slope variance.

I have considered plotting the intercept and, at that point only,
putting the broad inference CI error bars.  Then, I could plot the
narrow inference effect around the regression line.  However, there
doesn't seem to be a way to place such bars without being misleading.
They certainly can't all start at the same intercept, that implies
increasing variability in measurement over time (and increasing
accuracy back in time).  But, what's the alternative because the
intercept and slope our now separate?

(BTW, the curved error bars in regression seem problematic in any
event because if the slope variance is very high with a small
intercept variance then it implies somewhere about the middle of the
line there is this artificially very high accuracy)

______________________________________________

<ja...@freelancepropaganda.com> wrote:

> Interesting plan, I'd probably use something like this, although white

>

> be able to get close with
>
> + scale_area(to=c(0,23))
>
> but I have no idea why 23ish is the right factor there ...

The problem is trying to match up the scale of the points (measured in
mm) to the scale of the plot (which can be any arbitrary size).  To
solve this problem you really need a circle geom that operates
entirely with data units (i.e. the circles would radius 1 data unit),
but it's not obvious to me what generality this geom should have:

 * should you specify just the radius, or should it be possible to
draw ovals as will?
 * if it should, how should they be parameterised?  with
variance-covariance matrix?

It's probably not really a lot of work, but I haven't had time to
think about it properly.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christian,

Maybe something like this?  The key is to do the sorting and
computation of x value on a per year basis.

library(plyr)
d <- data.frame(
  year = factor(floor(rnorm(50,2005,2))),
  visits = floor(rpois(50,3))
)

d2 <- ddply(d, "year", function(df) {
  df <- df[order(df$visits), ]
  df$n <- 1:nrow(df)
  df
})

library(ggplot2)
qplot(n, visits, data = d2, colour = year, geom = "step")

Hadley

messages.subject: [ANN] ggplot2 version 0.8.3
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot2 is a plotting system for R, based on the grammar of graphics,
which tries to take the good parts of base and lattice graphics and
avoid bad parts. It takes care of many of the fiddly details
that make plotting a hassle (like drawing legends) as well as
providing a powerful model of graphics that makes it easy to produce
complex multi-layered graphics.

To install or update, run:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "plyr"))

Find out more at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2, and check out the nearly 500
examples of ggplot in use.  If you're interested, you can also sign up to
the ggplot2 mailing list at http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2, or track
development at  http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2

ggplot2 0.8.3  (2008-04-20)
----------------------------------------

New features

* alpha: new aesthetic, with scale alpha.  Where a geom has both fill
and colour, alpha affects the fill.
* annotate: new annotate function to make it easier to add annotations to plots
* facet_grid now takes strip label function from parameter labeller,
not theme setting
* facet_grid: gains as.table argument to control direction of horizontal facets
* fortify: full set of methods for turning data from the sp package
into data frames that can be plotted with ggplot2
* geom_errorbarh: new geom for horizontal error bars
* labels_parsed and labels_bquote functions to make it easier to
display expressions on facet labels
* scale_manual now supports breaks and limits
* subset: experimental new feature.  Layers now have a subset
argument, which takes subsets formatted like .(var1 < 5, var2 == 3)
etc.
* xlim and ylim now work recognise Date and POSIXct classes to create
date and date_time scales respectively

Dealing with missing values

* facet_wrap: add drop argument to control whether or not panels for
non-existent combinations of facetting variables should be dropped or
not.  Defaults to TRUE
* scale_discrete: empty factor levels will be preserved, unless drop = TRUE

Bug fixes

* added presidents dataset from book to package
* American spelling of color accepted in as geom parameter, and all
colour scales have alias spelled color (e.g. scale_color_hue)
* facet_wrap: contents guaranteed to be clipped to panel
* facet_wrap: corrected labelling when facetting by multiple variables
(thank to Charlotte Wickham for a clear test case)
* geom_histogram now works with negative weights (provided position =
"identity").  This is useful for creating back to back histograms.
* geom_step: improve legend
* geom_text: better legend
* geom_vline, geom_hline, geom_abline: should work in yet more situations
* resolution: fixed bug in computation of resolution that lead to
(e.g.) incorrect boxplot widths when there was only a single x value
in a group.
* position_stack: fixed bug in detection of overlap for very large bins
* scale_discrete: factor levels no longer mistakenly reordered
* scale_hue: now spans full range of hue if it less than 360 degrees
* scale_hue: rotated default hue range by 15 degrees to avoid
unfortunate red-green contrast in two colour case
* show now works with ggplot objects
* stat_sum: fixed bug which resulted in dropped aesthetics
* stat_summary: now warns when dropping records with missing values
* stat_summary: should be a little faster
* stat_summary: correctly passes ... arguments on fun.data
* theme_bw: corrected justification of axis.text.y
* trans: bug fixes to logistic transformation
* order aesthetic should work again

--
http://had.co.nz/

Here's an example.  Suppose I'm measuring traffic passing some
particular point.  T is the time I detect a car and E is its speed.  I
want to know the amount of traffic intensity (geom_density) and I want
a scatterplot of speed, both plotted against time, something like:

ggplot(zz,aes(x=T))+geom_density()+geom_point(aes(x=T,y=E))

Of course, the vertical scales for density and for speed need to be
different. I can't find secondary axis scales
in the doc right now, but they must be there somewhere....

By the way, I might also want a scatterplot of speed vs. traffic
intensity, but that's no longer a job for geom_stat, but for
preprocessing....

messages.subject: Re: Survival-Analysis-Plots with grouped line-plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

Here are some ideas to get you started:

library(survival)

# Fit a basic model
fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ x, data=aml)
# See what the existing plot looks like
plot(fit)
# Look at the code to produce that plot:
survival:::plot.survfit
# it's a nightmare, as is most plotting code in R.

# Let's take a look at what's in the fit object
str(fit)
# ?survfit.object is helpful for understand this

# Let's convert this into a data frame we can use as input
# to ggplot etc.

df <- data.frame(
  time = fit$time,
  n.risk = fit$n.risk,
  n.event = fit$n.event,
  surv = fit$surv,
  strata = rep(levels(aml$x), fit$ntimes.strata),
  upper = fit$upper,
  lower = fit$lower
)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(df, aes(time, surv, colour = strata)) + geom_step()

# Missing the zeros, so add those in
zeros <- data.frame(time = 0, surv = 1, strata = levels(aml$x),
  upper = 1, lower = 1)
df <- rbind.fill(zeros, df)

ggplot(df, aes(time, surv, colour = strata)) + geom_step()

# We could also add in error bars
# Note that I'm using the new alpha aesthetic here which requires
# the latest version of ggplot2
ggplot(df, aes(time, surv, colour = strata)) + geom_step() +
  geom_step(aes(y = upper), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_step(aes(y = lower), alpha = 0.5)

# Which might be better with faceting
last_plot() + facet_wrap(~ strata)
# or maybe
last_plot() + facet_grid(. ~ strata, scales = "free_x", space = "free")

Hadley

messages.subject: Bug in annotate() with histograms: renames y axis label from "count" to "y"
messages.subject_clean: Bug in annotate() with histograms: renames y axis label from "count" to "y"
messages.body_plain:
The annotate function is very useful - and thanks Hadley for adding
it. However, I've found that using annotate() changes the y axis label
in a histogram from "count" to "y".

# Generate some numbers
df <- data.frame(first=rnorm(100), second=rnorm(100))

# Histogram: y axis labeled "count"
qplot(first, data=df)
# This changes the axis label from "count" to "y"
qplot(first, data=df) + annotate("text",x=1,y=1,label="my annotation")

# No effect on scatterplot
qplot(first, second, data=df) + annotate("text",x=1,y=1,label="my
annotation")

Also, in histogram, is it possible to rename the y axis from "count"
to something else, or make it go away entirely? Setting ylab doesn't
do anything, which I guess makes sense since the y axis is generated
by counting up the data.

If this forum isn't the right place to report bugs, please let me know
where they should go. I've been running into little ones here and
there as I've gotten familiar with ggplot2.

-Winston

messages.subject: Standard deviation and stacked barcharts
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a small plotting challenge for the ggploters out there (I'll be
specific in presenting it because it is clearer):

I have replicated counts of some organisms, classified in size
fractions, at different depths. I want to plot a graph that would
represent simultaneously:
   - the proportion of each size fraction
   - the total amount at each depth
   - the variance in the abundance of each of these categories and
possibly of the total

My initial guess was to use stacked barcharts to represent both the
relative abundance of each size fraction and the total amount. But I
can't find a legible way to put standard deviation for each size
fraction on such a graph. What would you do? Is there something that
takes care of that already in ggplot?

Code example:

# count data
datCounts = data.frame(depth=c(rep(10,10), rep(20,10)),
class=rep(c(rep("<3",5), rep(">3",5)),2), abund=c(runif(10),
runif(10)*2))
#  the goal is to compare the profile of some governing parameter to
the abundances of the organisms, this is the profile
datProfile = data.frame(depth=0:30, value=(rnorm(31)))

# split the view
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(nrow=1, ncol=3)))

# plot the profile
p1 = ggplot(datProfile) + geom_path(aes(x=-depth, y=value)) +
coord_flip()
print(p1, vp=viewport(layout.pos.row=1, layout.pos.col=1))

# plot the abundances on the same scale
p2 = ggplot(datCounts) +
   geom_bar(mapping=aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
binwidth=1) +
   scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) +
   coord_flip()
print(p2, vp=viewport(layout.pos.row=1, layout.pos.col=2))
# the use of stacked bar charts gives information on both the total
abundance at each depth and the composition of the assemblage. In
addition, the bars are thin enough to situate them well in depth,
which is useful for the comparison with the profile. However the
abundances obviously vary in time and place, and what is represented
is currently just the sum.
# how could I plot the mean and add standard deviation to this kind of
plot?

# one possiblity would be to dodge bars instead of stacking them but
then the total abundance is not as obvious:
datSummary = ddply(datCounts, .(depth, class), function(x){
   data.frame(mean=mean(x$abund), sd=sd(x$abund))
})
p3 = ggplot(datSummary, aes(x=-depth)) +
   geom_bar(aes(y=mean, fill=class), binwidth=1, position="dodge",
stat="identity") +
   scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymax=(mean+sd),ymin=(mean-sd)), position="dodge",
width=2) +
   coord_flip()
print(p3, vp=viewport(layout.pos.row=1, layout.pos.col=3))

# result: http://jo.irisson.free.fr/dropbox/bar_errorbar.png

# Additional remarks (which I am sure Hadley is well aware of, but
just in case...):

# 1/ bindiwdth does not work in the last construction of geom_bar,
with stat="identity". I agree it does not make much sense when there
is just one value but there should probably still be a way to control
the width of the bar.

# 2/ The way to add error bars to such a bar chart kind of looks like
a hack. Fortunately plyr makes it easy to compute the summary stats.
But the use of stat="identity" with just one value seems "hacky" and
the placement of the bars when width is specified (as emphasized here)
is sub-optimal. I would expect that to be just an option in most of
ggplot geoms, like errorbar=TRUE, or errorbar="sd"/"se"/"none"

# 3/ there seem to be a quirk in the placement of bars in geom_bar:
ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
binwidth=4) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
# --> bars correctly centered on 10 and 20
ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
binwidth=2) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
# --> bars _starting_ on 10 and 20, but not centered while they could
easily be since the binwidth is even.

Thanks in advance for you help.

Jean-Olivier Irisson

I see the issue here... I put the ylab in the qplot arguments instead of alone. I don't know if this is the expected behavior or not.

# Label works
qplot(first, data=df) + annotate("text",x=1,y=1,label="my annotation") + ylab("foo")

# Label doesn't work
qplot(first, data=df, ylab="foo") + annotate("text",x=1,y=1,label="my annotation")

This doesn't touch on the issue of annotate() renaming the y axis from "count" to "y", of course.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Memory error with ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Well, that is a big surface to do a density estimation on.

You are probably just running out of memory. You can diagnose it a bit
better by knowing that
   gc()
will report how much memory you have used in a session. (so do it with
your small, working examples and then run gc). You can do this for a
couple of example sizes and see how memory scales with number of rows.
Additionally, you might want to know if your version of R is 64bit (do
a .Machine$sizeof.pointer - if that has the value 8 you are 64 bit, if
it has the value 4 you are are 32 bit).

You probably need to re-think your computation.

Kasper

On Sun, Apr 26, 2009 at 10:32 AM, Herbert Jägle
<herbert...@uni-tuebingen.de> wrote:
>
> So both methods should work. However, why does the following code not
> work?

Because you're using a non-standard construction - the following is
much to be preferred:

p <- ggplot(bs, aes(DoI, X30Hz_A,colour=Eye)) +

  labs(x="Date of investigation") +

  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,120)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ PID)

(it's also quite a bit shorter!)

The problem is in your code there's not enough information to figure
out what the x scale will be until just before the data is plotted,
and the way labs() works requires the scale to already be present
(this should be fixed in a future version).

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: geom_density error: object "y" not found
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Apr 21, 2009 at 2:28 PM, Stavros Macrakis <macr...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Well, actually it should be a geom_point.
>
> Here's an example.  Suppose I'm measuring traffic passing some
> particular point.  T is the time I detect a car and E is its speed.  I
> want to know the amount of traffic intensity (geom_density) and I want
> a scatterplot of speed, both plotted against time, something like:
>
> ggplot(zz,aes(x=T))+geom_density()+geom_point(aes(x=T,y=E))
>
> Of course, the vertical scales for density and for speed need to be
> different. I can't find secondary axis scales
> in the doc right now, but they must be there somewhere....

There are no secondary scales in ggplot2, and I don't currently have
any intention of adding them, because of the way they distort the
data.

I don't see any particularly easy way to work around this.  Your best
bet would be to calculate the density yourself with density() and then
scale it to match your other x variable.  I'm not sure how useful a
plot this will create, however.

Yes.  The theoretical reason that I don't like multiple y scales is
because there is no longer a unique mapping between position and data
value.  The practical implication of this is that it's essentially
impossible to compare two series because you can arbitrarily change
their relationship by differences in scaling.

> alternative is presumably to stack the two graphs, one over the other,
> and let the user try to see correlations by lining them up by eye?

Well, I'd recommend a scatterplot.  But if you could provide a bit
more data I could offer more concrete suggestions.

Hadley

messages.subject: overlaying geom_boxplot() with geom_point
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have the following table:

head(res)

  ID       TF  TIME   VAL    PAR
1     1     X       2     -0.52   1.02
2     1     X       4      0.75   2.23
3     1     Y       2      1.45   1.32
4     1     Y       4      0.84   1.88
5     2     X       2      1.66   1.02
6     2     X       4      3.07   2.23

First, I'm plotting a set of stacked boxplots of VAL for each TF/TIME
combination and this works fine:

p = ggplot(data=res)+
          geom_boxplot(aes(x=factor(TF), y=VAL, fill=factor(TIME)))

Now I'm trying to overlay each boxplot with a set of points
corresponding to another parameter, PAR, so I do:

p + geom_point(aes(x=factor(TF),y=MEDIAN, colour=factor(TIME))

Ideally, I would like the X coordinate of the points to coincide with
the centres of the boxplots.
With the default parameters of position to geom_boxplot, setting
fill=factor(TIME) automatically shifts the boxplots so they are
positioned next to each other. The code above obviously does not take
this shift into account and so the X coordinate is the same for both
levels of factor(TIME).
Is there any way to tell geom_point to shift the X coordinate
accordingly?

Actually, perhaps geom_point() isn't even the best way of plotting
this, because (as you may have noticed above) there's actually only a
single value of PAR for each TF/TIME combination - ie, one per
boxplot. What I currently do is just plot loads of PAR points on top
of each other. So if there's a different function suitable for this
purpose, which can better handle the shift in position, this would be
as good.

Many thanks,
Mikhail

--
Mikhail Spivakov, PhD
European Molecular Biology Laboratory

messages.subject: coord_cartesian with dates, date/times
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to use coord_cartesian to zoom in on a part of a time
series, but cannot seem to do it.

Taking a similar example to Hadley's from the ggplot2 web pages:

df <- data.frame(date = seq(Sys.Date(), len=100, by="1 day")[sample
(100, 50)], price = runif(50))
df <- df[order(df$date), ]
qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line")

plots a nice time series.

To extract part of it, which also works:

qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line") + scale_x_date(limits = c
(as.Date("2009-04-27"), as.Date("2009-06-09")))

But what if I just want to zoom in on a date range (scale_x_date will
drop data outside the range)?  I had thought this would work:

qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line") + coord_cartesian(xlim = c
(as.Date("2009-04-27"), as.Date("2009-06-09")))

but returns the error:
Error in `-.Date`(x, from[1]) : Can only subtract from Date objects

Does coord_cartesian work with Date or POSIXct classes, or am I
missing something?  It would be nice if it did.

Thanks!

David

On Mon, Apr 27, 2009 at 2:58 PM,  <d.c.c...@its.leeds.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> Dear all,
>
> I would like to use coord_cartesian to zoom in on a part of a time
> series, but cannot seem to do it.
>
> Taking a similar example to Hadley's from the ggplot2 web pages:
>
> df <- data.frame(date = seq(Sys.Date(), len=100, by="1 day")[sample
> (100, 50)], price = runif(50))
> df <- df[order(df$date), ]
> qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line")
>
> plots a nice time series.
>
> To extract part of it, which also works:
>
> qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line") + scale_x_date(limits = c
> (as.Date("2009-04-27"), as.Date("2009-06-09")))
>
> But what if I just want to zoom in on a date range (scale_x_date will
> drop data outside the range)?  I had thought this would work:
>
> qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line") + coord_cartesian(xlim = c
> (as.Date("2009-04-27"), as.Date("2009-06-09")))

Try this:

coord_cartesian(xlim = as.numeric(as.Date(c("2009-04-27", "2009-06-09"))))

By the time the date gets to the coordinate system, it has been
converted to a numeric, so coord_cartesian needs numeric limits.  In
an ideal world, you'd be able to zoom in by just dragging the mouse
around, so it wouldn't be a problem.  Unfortunately R graphics doesn't
make that easy.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Standard deviation and stacked barcharts
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately I don't have any ideas for the presentation, but I can
at least answer these questions.

> # Additional remarks (which I am sure Hadley is well aware of, but just in
> case...):
>
> # 1/ bindiwdth does not work in the last construction of geom_bar, with
> stat="identity". I agree it does not make much sense when there is just one
> value but there should probably still be a way to control the width of the
> bar.

binwidth controls the binning performed by stat_bin, so you shouldn't
expect it to work when stat="identity".  width should control the
physical width of the bars in that case.

> # 2/ The way to add error bars to such a bar chart kind of looks like a
> hack. Fortunately plyr makes it easy to compute the summary stats. But the
> use of stat="identity" with just one value seems "hacky" and the placement
> of the bars when width is specified (as emphasized here) is sub-optimal. I
> would expect that to be just an option in most of ggplot geoms, like
> errorbar=TRUE, or errorbar="sd"/"se"/"none"

I'm not completely sure what you're referring to here, but maybe the
examples in position_dodge will help with the alignment.  There's no
built in support for calculating errors, mainly because there are so
many different ways to do it, depending on the underlying model.
Usually, it's easy enough to do with plyr, and then your calculations
are explicit, and easy to check.

> # 3/ there seem to be a quirk in the placement of bars in geom_bar:
> ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
> binwidth=4) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
> # --> bars correctly centered on 10 and 20
> ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
> binwidth=2) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
> # --> bars _starting_ on 10 and 20, but not centered while they could easily
> be since the binwidth is even.

The bars show the interval that the counts where binned over.  For you
example, you could do

 ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=depth, fill=class), binwidth=2, origin = 1)

to have the bins centered on even numbers.

Hadley

--

messages.subject: Re: Standard deviation and stacked barcharts
messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for your reply Hadley.

On 2009-April-28  , at 14:16 , hadley wickham wrote:

> Unfortunately I don't have any ideas for the presentation, but I can
> at least answer these questions.

OK, too bad then. I guess the problem of this graph is really that it
tries to show too many things at once rather than some limitation in
the plotting program.
More generally, it seems that barcharts (and stacked barcharts in
particular) are most often used in histogram-like constructs, where
the height of the bars is proportional to the _sum_ of some counts, so
there is no variance involved in that, hence no need for error bars.

>> # 1/ bindiwdth does not work in the last construction of geom_bar,
>> with
>> stat="identity". I agree it does not make much sense when there is
>> just one
>> value but there should probably still be a way to control the width
>> of the
>> bar.
>
> binwidth controls the binning performed by stat_bin, so you shouldn't
> expect it to work when stat="identity".  width should control the
> physical width of the bars in that case.

Indeed it was stupid of me to try binwidth since stat_bin is probably
not even called ;)

However, "width" is also an aesthetic of stat_bin, not of
stat_identity or geom_bar. So it should not work either. But it does.
In a strange way:

datCounts = data.frame(depth=c(rep(10,10), rep(20,10)),
class=rep(c(rep("<3",5), rep(">3",5)),2), abund=c(runif(10),
runif(10)*2))
datSummary = ddply(datCounts, .(depth, class), function(x){
data.frame(mean=mean(x$abund), sd=sd(x$abund))
})
# that does not work
ggplot(datSummary, aes(x=-depth)) + geom_bar(aes(y=mean, fill=class),
width=1, position="dodge", stat="identity") +
scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0))
# but that works
ggplot(datSummary, aes(x=-depth)) + geom_bar(aes(y=mean, fill=class,
width=1), position="dodge", stat="identity") +
scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0))

I would have expected "width" to be a parameter and not an aesthetic
in this case, since I fix it to a constant instead of mapping it to a
variable. I guess the difference is that, as an aesthetic, it gets
passed to the underlying stat function. But then, stat_identity does
not take any arguments...

>> # 2/ The way to add error bars to such a bar chart kind of looks
>> like a
>> hack. Fortunately plyr makes it easy to compute the summary stats.
>> But the
>> use of stat="identity" with just one value seems "hacky" and the
>> placement
>> of the bars when width is specified (as emphasized here) is sub-
>> optimal. I
>> would expect that to be just an option in most of ggplot geoms, like
>> errorbar=TRUE, or errorbar="sd"/"se"/"none"
>
> I'm not completely sure what you're referring to here, but maybe the
> examples in position_dodge will help with the alignment.

I am referring to the fact that, when width is not the same in
geom_bar and geom_errorbar the error bars are not centered on the bar.
This is the case when "width" is specified in either geom_bar or
geom_errorbar with a value different from the default, or in both but
with different values.

p= ggplot(datSummary, aes(x=-depth)) +
geom_bar(aes(y=mean, fill=class, width=4), position="dodge",
stat="identity") +
scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0))
p + geom_errorbar(aes(ymax=(mean+sd),ymin=(mean-sd)), width=2,
position="dodge")

Indeed the doc for position_dodge helps and this works:

p + geom_errorbar(aes(ymax=(mean+sd),ymin=(mean-sd)), width=2,
position=position_dodge(width=4))

My problem probably came from not realizing that errorbar is a geom in
itself, completely independent of whatever you draw underneath. So, if
I want the two layers to match, I have to deal with the placement
myself. I guess I was spoiled by the rest of ggplot which usually
deals with this kind of graphical alignment for you. Plus, error bars
are rarely drawn by themselves. Conceptually, they often complement
another geom rather than being a geom per se. So one could expect them
to be automatically aligned to whatever they complement.

I am probably still not very clear...

NB: setting the width parameter as a general aesthetic in the ggplot
call helps synchronizing all the widths:

ggplot(datSummary, aes(x=-depth, width=6)) +
geom_bar(aes(y=mean, fill=class), position="dodge", stat="identity") +
scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) +
geom_errorbar(aes(ymax=(mean+sd),ymin=(mean-sd)), position="dodge")

> There's no
> built in support for calculating errors, mainly because there are so
> many different ways to do it, depending on the underlying model.
> Usually, it's easy enough to do with plyr, and then your calculations
> are explicit, and easy to check.

OK, fair enough (I need to learn plyr anyway ;) )

>> # 3/ there seem to be a quirk in the placement of bars in geom_bar:
>> ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
>> binwidth=4) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
>> # --> bars correctly centered on 10 and 20
>> ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=-depth, weight=abund, fill=class),
>> binwidth=2) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-30,0)) + coord_flip()
>> # --> bars _starting_ on 10 and 20, but not centered while they
>> could easily
>> be since the binwidth is even.
>
> The bars show the interval that the counts where binned over.  For you
> example, you could do
>
> ggplot(datCounts) + geom_bar(aes(x=depth, fill=class), binwidth=2,
> origin = 1)
>
> to have the bins centered on even numbers.

Thanks. It works.

JiHO

messages.subject: Strange diagonals with plotmatrix for data frames with non-numeric variables
messages.subject_clean: Strange diagonals with plotmatrix for data frames with non-numeric variables
messages.body_plain:
Compare the output of

plotmatrix(iris[,1:4])

with the output of

plotmatrix(iris)

The diagonal panels should be identical for the four first variables,
but they aren’t. In the ‘plotmatrix(iris)’ example they show some
strange curves, while in the ‘plotmatrix(iris[,1:4])’ example they
(correctly) show density estimates.

--

messages.subject: help with converting for loop to vector operation
messages.subject_clean: help with converting for loop to vector operation
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I have a wrapper function that draws a graph that I'd like to use in a vector-like manner.  The for-loop version I currently use is as follows:

#----------------------------------------------------------
draw_metric_by_date <- function( df, i, smooth=FALSE, BASEPATH ) {
        mlabel  <- names(df)[i]
        qmetric <- qplot( data=df, x=date, y=d[,i], geom=c('line','jitter'), ylab=mlabel, main=mlabel, colour=I("dark blue") )

         if ( smooth == TRUE ) {
                print("smoother requested...")
                tmp     <- qmetric
                qmetric <- tmp + stat_smooth()
        }

        pngfn <- paste( BASEPATH, "/png/", mlabel, ".png", sep="")
        print(pngfn)
        png( file=pngfn, height=h, width=w )
                print(qmetric)
                dev.off()
}

for ( i in c(4:120 ) ) {
        print(names(d)[i])
        draw_metric_by_date( d, i, smooth=TRUE )
}

Could someone show me how to do the same with a vector approach with an "apply" function ?

Many thanks,
Avram

function for each of the two plots. In ggplot2, how do I tell it to
use different geoms for the two panels?

Damon.

messages.body_plain:
Try this perhaps,

dummy <- data.frame(x=seq(1, 10, length=100), y=rnorm(100),
type=factor(c("f1", "f2")))

d1 <- data.frame(x=1:10, y=sin(1:10), type="f1")
d2 <- data.frame(x=1:10, y=cos(1:10), type="f2")

ggplot(data = dummy, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
facet_grid(type~., scale="free") +
layer(data=d1,  geom = c( "line"), stat = "identity" ) +
layer(data=d2,  geom = c( "point"), stat = "identity" )

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
This is probably very basic information for many out there, but just in case...

To write out an object in a format that can be easily cut and pasted:
> dput(mk)
  [copy the output and paste into email message]

This generates output that the other person can just copy and paste into their R console to generate the correct data structure.

On the receiving end, even if the data has been pasted in a plain text format (as squid did earlier) rather than a nice R command format from dput(), it's still possible to read it in without too much trouble.

> mk <- read.table(file=stdin(), header=T)
 [paste table text here]

However, there's no guarantee that the types of each column will be correct; if the sender wants, for example, a column of numbers to be treated as a factor, that conversion needs to be done by hand.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: plots unaffected by alpha (mac)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ian -

On my mac the first command you provide plots (seemingly) nothing, and
the second plots the points fine.  The reason the first does not is
that the alpha level is too low, so if you enter

qplot(carat, price, data = diamonds, alpha = 1/50)

you should see the transparency.  I think Hadley told me that the
limit is 1/256, so that you have to stack 256 points on top of each
other to get the opaque color.  Now, in the new version (0.8.3) alpha
was added as an aesthetic as well, so if you want it can vary with the
data just as something like a size can (i.e., it doesn't have to be
fixed for every point like 1/256).

Make sure that you have the new version installed.
( install.packages('ggplot2') )

In any case, something like this should run without any problems -

ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price), data = diamonds) +
   geom_point(colour = alpha('black', 1/50))

Does that help?

david.

PS - if you installed the new version of ggplot2 more than a few days
ago, reinstall it; there were problems uploading versions to the CRAN
which were recently fixed.

messages.subject: legend associated to geom_pointrange
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using geom_pointrange to create a scatter plot for several
conditions that I map to different colors. The problem I have is that
the legend shows thick lines that dont look very good. I want to plot
points in the legend for example.

I can use geom_point and geom_linerange separately including
legend=FALSE for the last one, but the problem is that I am using
jittering to avoid overplotting and naturally the jitter for the
points and error bars should be the same so I guess I cannot use these
to geoms separately.

The following toy code shows the thick lines in the legend I am
talking about:

df<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(2,3),ymin=c(1.8,2.7),ymax=c(2.2,3.1))
p<-ggplot(data=df,aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=ymin,ymax=ymax,color="condition"))
p + geom_pointrange()

thanks

dani

--
Daniel Linares

messages.subject: How to plot only subjects with multiple observations?
messages.subject_clean: How to plot only subjects with multiple observations?
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I have a data frame that has data on about 25 people on about 20 variables of interest.
Each person is measured up to 10 times, but some people are measured only once or twice,
and, even for the people who are measured more times, some variables are missing for nearly
all cases.

I am exploring the data using qplot:

qplot(days, C3a, facets = ~Patient_Name, data = multvisit, geom = c("point", "smooth"),
 main = 'C3a over time in people with more than 2 visits',
 xlab = 'Days since 9/25/06')

but this produces plots for all people.  How can I produce plots just for people with 3 or
more non-missing observations?

thanks

Peter

Peter L. Flom, PhD
Statistical Consultant

> qplot(start, FETpvalueM_MSmin2, data=subset(mk,

Try this code:

qplot(start, FETpvalueM_MSmin2, facets = arm ~ ., data = mk) +
  geom_text(aes(label=file), size = 4, hjust = 1, vjust = 1) +
  ylim(0, 0.05)

The problem is that you were missing the aes call in geom_text and you
had previously used attach, so ggplot2 used the file variable from the
global environment, causing the issue you saw.

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: How to plot only subjects with multiple observations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

You could use plyr to add a column that counts the number of
observations and then subset on that:

multvisit <- ddply(multvisit, "Patient_Name", transform, n = sum(is.na <http://is.na>(C3a))
subset(multvisit, n > 3)

If you have many columns like this, it might be easier to melt the
data first, then compute the counts

multm <- melt(multvisit, id = c("Patient_Name", "days"), na.rm = T)
multm <- ddply(mult, c("Patient_Name", "days"), transform, n = seq_along(days))

qplot(days, value, data = subset(multm, n > 3 && variable == "C3a"))

Hadley

messages.subject: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.subject_clean: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.body_plain:
In current ggplot2, a Boolean variable's legend looks like a factor's legend where the values are TRUE and FALSE, something like this:

Weekday
   X  TRUE
   Y  FALSE

(where X and Y are the keys).  This is all perfectly logical and consistent, but I think it would be more elegant and helpful if it looked like:

X  Weekday
Y  ~Weekday

(no legend title) or

X  Weekday
Y  other

And if it is going to remain with a legend title, it might be more user friendly to translate the ugly all-caps TRUE -> Yes, FALSE -> No.

          -s

messages.subject: Re: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.subject_clean: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stavros -

It seems to me like for each instance you can simply change the labels, like

a <- rep(c(TRUE,FALSE), 50)
qplot(a, data = data.frame(a = a), geom = 'bar', fill = a) +
  scale_fill_discrete('', labels = c('t','f'))

or whatever you might prefer; so the question is more the default.  One of the disadvantages of the other methods you listed is that in many cases it will widen the legend box and make the plot smaller.  So the current default seems pretty reasonable to me.

On the other hand, you have a good point with the TRUE/FALSE labels, but I think True/False is probably a better default.  I hadn't really noticed it before. :)

cheers
david.

messages.subject: Re: data going to wrong facet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley,

Thanks very much for this. Naturally it leads to several follow up
questions...

1. Is it generally inappropriate and/or unnecessary to "attach"?  Are
there any rules of thumb for this?

2. I'm now working with this dataset using melt which going really
well for the most part. Great function! But now that I'm working with
this modified dataset, I have cases where I'd like to plot subsets of
subsets of data. The "melted" dataset I'm working with has 854701 rows
so I'm not going to paste it here but I can put it up in files if
necessary. I think the question might be straightforward enough
without having to work through it though.
In this melted dataset,  there are 2 relevant descriptor terms
(measure and inSpecies) that are connected to values:

> summary(rm$measure)
analyzedCodons      FETpvalue           Nfix          Npoly
NpolyShare
         61050         146520          73260         146520
73260
          Sfix          Spoly     SpolyShare    totalCodons
         73260         146520          73260          61050
> summary(rm$inSpecies)
     M     MP     MS      P      S     SP
146520 146520 122100 146520 146520 146520

I can plot the subset of the data that only looks at the measure
FETpvalue as you suggested above by

qplot(start, value, data=subset(rm, measure="FETpvalue"),
colour=inSpecies, facets=arm~.) +

  geom_text(aes(label=file), size = 4, hjust = 1, vjust = 1) +
  ylim(0, 0.05)

but how do I look at only the values of that variable that fall within
a certain range? FETpvalue is a pvalue, so for example, only things
less than 0.01. Is there a way to do it internally rather than by
setting a ylim as you do?  Previously, I was using

qplot(start, FETpvalueM_MSmin2, data=subset(mk,
FETpvalueM_MSmin2<0.05)) but I can't see how to do this now that I'm
using the melted dataset.

3. For a more complex scenario, I've been able to plot several subsets
of the data as follows:
data=subset(rm, measure==c("Nfix","FETpvalue"))  but is it possible to
also put restrictions on the values of each these variables as above
for pvalue? For example, how would I plot only data points where
measure=FETpvalue <0.05 and measure=Nfix>5?

4. Even more complex, is it possible to put multiple restrictions on
both variables? e.g.,  plot only the subset where measure=
FETpvalue<0.01 AND inSpecies=M?

5. And finally, is it possible to  plot different relationships of the
variables, for example Nfix/Sfix?

Many thanks, once again.
Mara

geom_vline(xintercept=c
(18930000,26764357,31450000,82024058,103665182))

categorical variable (yes vs no). I'm still curious how to make
several different color backgrounds in between a few of the vertical
lines I've drawn so it would be easier to distinguish which
"Inversion" is which. Between 18930000 and 26764357 is inversion 1,
between 26764357 and 31450000 is inversion 2, and between 82024058 and

to plot them as an addition on each figure rather than needing
something that can read an actual variable, so if anyone has any great
ideas, thanks.

Mara.

> qplot(start, FETpvalueM_MSmin2, data=subset(mk,
> FETpvalueM_MSmin2<0.05)) but I can't see how to do this now that I'm
> using the melted dataset.

You'd just do subset(rm, measure == "FETpvalue" & value < 0.05)

> 3. For a more complex scenario, I've been able to plot several subsets
> of the data as follows:
> data=subset(rm, measure==c("Nfix","FETpvalue"))  but is it possible to
> also put restrictions on the values of each these variables as above
> for pvalue? For example, how would I plot only data points where
> measure=FETpvalue <0.05 and measure=Nfix>5?

(measure == "FETpvalue" & value < 0.05) | (measure == "Nfix" & value > 5)

But it may be better to just stick with the raw data.

> 4. Even more complex, is it possible to put multiple restrictions on
> both variables? e.g.,  plot only the subset where measure=
> FETpvalue<0.01 AND inSpecies=M?

See above for the basic idea.

> 5. And finally, is it possible to  plot different relationships of the
> variables, for example Nfix/Sfix?

No - you'd want to use the non-molten data for that.

Hadley

messages.subject: Combination of stacking and dodging
messages.body_plain:
Hi @all :-),

I recently search for a beautiful solution to display stacked bars
(for a certain variable) in a bar-chart side by side for different
groups (dodges).
My task is to show the comparison of a variable of one type of subject
compared with the values of all types of subjects (the compared
included) together.
The first approach was to solve it with facets. I considered that as
pretty nice, on the upper half of the window you can see the overall-
rates and on the lower half the evaluation of only one subject. But
the customer is not satisfied with that solution (though it is an
uncommercial project :-D). All in all, what I need is a combination of
the "position=stack" and "position=dodge" functionality. Hadley, I
have read a discussion between you and another user, who got exactly
the same question. But that was on october 25th 2008. Maybe there is
an easier solution for it now ? I see, that I could easily solve it
with aes(x=as.numeric(variable) + *shifting*)). But is there an
approach integrated in the proper use of ggplot2 ? Some new parameter
for facetting ? Excuse me, if I oversaw that fact in the ggplot2 -
book. What I am searching for is simply stack-dodging :-).

Sorry, if I stole your time.

Best Regards,

Edgar

messages.subject: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.subject_clean: Legend title and key label for boolean variables
messages.body_plain:
Yes, it is just a suggested change to the default presentation, and I agree that it potentially makes the legend box bigger.
ggplot2 is so beautiful in so many ways that this seems like a reasonable sort of tweak....

            -s

On Thu, Apr 30, 2009 at 12:17 PM, David Kahle <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Stavros -
>
> It seems to me like for each instance you can simply change the labels, like
>
> a <- rep(c(TRUE,FALSE), 50)
> qplot(a, data = data.frame(a = a), geom = 'bar', fill = a) +
>   scale_fill_discrete('', labels = c('t','f'))
>
> or whatever you might prefer; so the question is more the default.  One of the disadvantages of the other methods you listed is that in many cases it will widen the legend box and make the plot smaller.  So the current default seems pretty reasonable to me.
>
> On the other hand, you have a good point with the TRUE/FALSE labels, but I think True/False is probably a better default.  I hadn't really noticed it before. :)
>
> cheers
> david.
>
>
> On Apr 30, 2009, at 10:47 AM, Stavros Macrakis wrote:
>
> > In current ggplot2, a Boolean variable's legend looks like a factor's legend where the values are TRUE and FALSE, something like this:
> >
> > Weekday
> >    X  TRUE
> >    Y  FALSE
> >
> > (where X and Y are the keys).  This is all perfectly logical and consistent, but I think it would be more elegant and helpful if it looked like:
> >
> > X  Weekday
> > Y  ~Weekday
> >
> > (no legend title) or
> >
> > X  Weekday
> > Y  other
> >
> > And if it is going to remain with a legend title, it might be more user friendly to translate the ugly all-caps TRUE -> Yes, FALSE -> No.
> >
> >           -s
> >
> >
>
